PWs are constructed of one to three syllables². They are of two general contrastive classes: ultimate stress and penultimate stress³. 1.11 Ultimate Stress. All possible ultimate stress PWs may be derived from the following schematic string (where S = syllable and ´ = stress): (S) S) Ś. Monosyllabic and disyllabic PWs are derived from this formula. new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (van der Wilden & van der Wilden 1975: two contrastive PW classes, ultimate vs penultimate stress) and adds detail from the same author 33 years later: the two classes are 'equally represented'; unstressed pretonic vowels centralize while stressed vowels are low, so stress is recoverable from vowel quality ('highly predictable', hence unmarked in the 2007 orthography); c. 30 exceptions; minimal pair segi vs 'segi; V-initial words stress initial /a/ but not initial /i u/. The 'highly predictable' wording could be read as quality-driven stress rather than lexical stress, but the author still calls the two classes contrasting phonological word classes and marks s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are 1-3 syllables and fall into two 'equally represented', contrasting phonological word classes: pretonic-reduced + stressed final (C Ă.'CV(C), e.g. [dǝ'mu] 'stone', [kǝ'bɔŋ] 'die') versus stressed initial + full low vowel ('CÁ.CV(C), e.g. ['damɔy] 'full', ['gabE] 'exist here'). Stress correlates with vowel quality: stressed syllables have low vocoids [a E O], unstressed (pretonic) vocoids are high/centralized [ǝ]; in trisyllables stress is on the syllable with a low vocoid (e.g. [dǝ'manɔn] 'branch', [bǝ'tɔdɔp] 'hair'); in V-initial words initial /a/ is stressed ('aya 'father') while initial /i u/ are unstressed (i'mot 'we', u'dui 'banana'). Because of this correlation the author calls stress 'highly predictable' from the segmental shape and the practical orthography does not write it, but about 30 exceptional words exist and the dictionary writes a stress mark where the vowel letters do not decide it (orthographic e = [ǝ] or [E]), with the minimal pair segi [sǝ'gi] 'name of mountain' vs 'segi ['sEgi] 'complain'. So placement (final vs penult/initial) is a lexical property of the word, phonetically cued by full vs reduced vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Only 30 cases have been found as exception on this rule' (stress then written in the dictionary entry, e.g. 'lemple, 'segi); V-initial words: /a/ stressed, /i u/ unstressed, no centralization; one quadrisyllabic exception [i.su.'a.li] 'cassowary'; Gresi (Klesi) dialectal influence gives sogo sogo so 'why' a different stress pattern [sogohó goso]; syllabic continuants (r s m n ŋ) occur only in pre-stress position.
new_statements.identity_note: The Kamus describes Kemtuik with 'Kemtuik proper' (villages Merem and Yanim) as the model dialect; other dialects Iwalom (Sabron, Mamda, Meikari) and Ikuoy (south of Lake Sentani) differ only slightly; data collected mainly in Merem from 1975, with additions by Michael Werner 1985-2000 and local contributors 2005-2007.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction. The catalog (van der Wilden & van der Wilden 1975) records two contrastive stress classes (ultimate vs penultimate). The newly read 2008 trial edition of van der Wilden's Kamus Kemtuik (same author) restates the two 'contrasting phonological word classes' (C Ă.'CV(C) vs 'CÁ.CV(C), 'equally represented') and adds that stressed syllables carry low vocoids while unstressed pretonic vocoids centralize, so that stress is 'highly predictable' from the segmental form and left unwritten in the orthography, with about 30 exceptions and a minimal pair segi [sǝ'gi] vs 'segi ['sEgi]. A reader who takes the vowel-quality correlation as primary could call this quality-conditioned rather than lexical stress; the author's own framing (contrasting word classes, lexical stress marks in the dictionary where spelling is ambiguous) keeps it compatible with the catalog's 'lexical' kind. The 1991 research-notes volume remains unread (no open copy).

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the primary and only phonology of Kemtuik (van der Wilden & van der Wilden 1975, Irian IV(3):31-60), which we hold as a papuaweb/the Internet Archive page-image scan; the deciding quotation (two contrastive stress classes, ultimate ((S)S)Ś vs penultimate (S)ŚS, with examples and notes 2, 3, 6, 7) is confirmed verbatim on pp. 32-33, 59-60. The lexical coding with a right-edge two-syllable window follows directly from the source's own statement and example lists (e.g. /mi.á/ vs /bÁ.nu/). No later phonology, grammar, dissertation or instrumental study exists per Glottolog, OLAC, Crossref and WALS; the only unheld descriptive works are the same authors' 1991 sketch+dictionary and 2012 dictionary, which might refine counts or per-word marking but are unlikely to overturn the classification.
